prompt: A ____ is the most basic element of GitHub. They're easiest to imagine as a project's folder. A ____ contains all of the project files (including documentation), and stores each file's revision history. Repositories can have multiple collaborators and can be either public or private.
explain: repository: A repository is the most basic element of GitHub. They're easiest to imagine as a project's folder.
explainFull: repository: A repository is the most basic element of GitHub. They're easiest to imagine as a project's folder. A repository contains all of the project files (including documentation), and stores each file's revision history. Repositories can have multiple collaborators and can be either public or private.

prompt: A ____, or "revision", is an individual change to a file (or set of files). When you make a ____ to save your work, Git creates a unique ID (a.k.a. the "SHA" or "hash") that allows you to keep record of the specific changes committed along with who made them and when. ____ usually contain a ____ message which is a brief description of what changes were made.
explain: commit: A commit, or "revision", is an individual change to a file (or set of files). When you make a commit to save your work, Git creates a unique ID (a.k.a.
explainFull: commit: A commit, or "revision", is an individual change to a file (or set of files). When you make a commit to save your work, Git creates a unique ID (a.k.a. the "SHA" or "hash") that allows you to keep record of the specific changes committed along with who made them and when. Commits usually contain a commit message which is a brief description of what changes were made.

prompt: A ____ is a parallel version of a repository. It is contained within the repository, but does not affect the primary or main ____ allowing you to work freely without disrupting the "live" version. When you've made the changes you want to make, you can merge your ____ back into the main ____ to publish your changes.
explain: branch: A branch is a parallel version of a repository. It is contained within the repository, but does not affect the primary or main branch allowing you to work freely without disrupting the "live" version.
explainFull: branch: A branch is a parallel version of a repository. It is contained within the repository, but does not affect the primary or main branch allowing you to work freely without disrupting the "live" version. When you've made the changes you want to make, you can merge your branch back into the main branch to publish your changes.

prompt: A ____ is a copy of a repository that lives on your computer instead of on a website's server somewhere, or the act of making that copy. When you make a ____, you can edit the files in your preferred editor and use Git to keep track of your changes without having to be online. The repository you cloned is still connected to the remote version so that you can push your local changes to the remote to keep them synced when you're online.
explain: clone: A clone is a copy of a repository that lives on your computer instead of on a website's server somewhere, or the act of making that copy. When you make a clone, you can edit the files in your preferred editor and use Git to keep track of your changes without having to be online.
explainFull: clone: A clone is a copy of a repository that lives on your computer instead of on a website's server somewhere, or the act of making that copy. When you make a clone, you can edit the files in your preferred editor and use Git to keep track of your changes without having to be online. The repository you cloned is still connected to the remote version so that you can push your local changes to the remote to keep them synced when you're online.

prompt: To ____ means to send your committed changes to a remote repository on GitHub.com. For instance, if you change something locally, you can ____ those changes so that others may access them.
explain: push: To push means to send your committed changes to a remote repository on GitHub.com. For instance, if you change something locally, you can push those changes so that others may access them.
explainFull: push: To push means to send your committed changes to a remote repository on GitHub.com. For instance, if you change something locally, you can push those changes so that others may access them.

prompt: ____ refers to when you are fetching in changes and merging them. For instance, if someone has edited the remote file you're both working on, you'll want to ____ in those changes to your local copy so that it's up to date. See also fetch.
explain: pull: Pull refers to when you are fetching in changes and merging them. For instance, if someone has edited the remote file you're both working on, you'll want to pull in those changes to your local copy so that it's up to date.
explainFull: pull: Pull refers to when you are fetching in changes and merging them. For instance, if someone has edited the remote file you're both working on, you'll want to pull in those changes to your local copy so that it's up to date. See also fetch.

prompt: When you use `git ____`, you're adding changes from the remote repository to your local working branch without committing them. Unlike `git pull`, fetching allows you to review changes before committing them to your local branch.
explain: fetch: When you use `git fetch`, you're adding changes from the remote repository to your local working branch without committing them. Unlike `git pull`, fetching allows you to review changes before committing them to your local branch.
explainFull: fetch: When you use `git fetch`, you're adding changes from the remote repository to your local working branch without committing them. Unlike `git pull`, fetching allows you to review changes before committing them to your local branch.

prompt: Merging takes the changes from one branch (in the same repository or from a fork), and applies them into another. This often happens as a "pull request" (which can be thought of as a request to ____), or via the command line. A ____ can be done through a pull request via the GitHub.com web interface if there are no conflicting changes, or can always be done via the command line.
explain: merge: Merging takes the changes from one branch (in the same repository or from a fork), and applies them into another. This often happens as a "pull request" (which can be thought of as a request to merge), or via the command line.
explainFull: merge: Merging takes the changes from one branch (in the same repository or from a fork), and applies them into another. This often happens as a "pull request" (which can be thought of as a request to merge), or via the command line. A merge can be done through a pull request via the GitHub.com web interface if there are no conflicting changes, or can always be done via the command line.

prompt: A difference that occurs between merged branches. ____ happen when people make different changes to the same line of the same file, or when one person edits a file and another person deletes the same file. The ____ must be resolved before you can merge the branches.
explain: merge conflict: A difference that occurs between merged branches. Merge conflicts happen when people make different changes to the same line of the same file, or when one person edits a file and another person deletes the same file.
explainFull: merge conflict: A difference that occurs between merged branches. Merge conflicts happen when people make different changes to the same line of the same file, or when one person edits a file and another person deletes the same file. The merge conflict must be resolved before you can merge the branches.

prompt: ____ are proposed changes to a repository submitted by a user and accepted or rejected by a repository's collaborators. Like issues, ____ each have their own discussion forum.
explain: pull request: Pull requests are proposed changes to a repository submitted by a user and accepted or rejected by a repository's collaborators. Like issues, pull requests each have their own discussion forum.
explainFull: pull request: Pull requests are proposed changes to a repository submitted by a user and accepted or rejected by a repository's collaborators. Like issues, pull requests each have their own discussion forum.

prompt: This is the version of a repository or branch that is hosted on a server, most likely GitHub.com. ____ versions can be connected to local clones so that changes can be synced.
explain: remote: This is the version of a repository or branch that is hosted on a server, most likely GitHub.com. Remote versions can be connected to local clones so that changes can be synced.
explainFull: remote: This is the version of a repository or branch that is hosted on a server, most likely GitHub.com. Remote versions can be connected to local clones so that changes can be synced.

prompt: The default upstream repository. Most projects have at least one upstream project that they track. By default, ____ is used for that purpose.
explain: origin: The default upstream repository. Most projects have at least one upstream project that they track.
explainFull: origin: The default upstream repository. Most projects have at least one upstream project that they track. By default, origin is used for that purpose.

prompt: The default development branch. Whenever you create a Git repository, a branch named `____` is created, and becomes the active branch. In most cases, this contains the local development, though that is purely by convention and is not required.
explain: main: The default development branch. Whenever you create a Git repository, a branch named `main` is created, and becomes the active branch.
explainFull: main: The default development branch. Whenever you create a Git repository, a branch named `main` is created, and becomes the active branch. In most cases, this contains the local development, though that is purely by convention and is not required.

prompt: The base branch for new pull requests and code commits in a repository. Each repository has at least one branch, which Git creates when you initialize the repository. The first branch is usually called `main`, and is often the ____.
explain: default branch: The base branch for new pull requests and code commits in a repository. Each repository has at least one branch, which Git creates when you initialize the repository.
explainFull: default branch: The base branch for new pull requests and code commits in a repository. Each repository has at least one branch, which Git creates when you initialize the repository. The first branch is usually called `main`, and is often the default branch.

prompt: Short, descriptive text that accompanies a commit and communicates the change the commit is introducing.
explain: commit message: Short, descriptive text that accompanies a commit and communicates the change the commit is introducing.
explainFull: commit message: Short, descriptive text that accompanies a commit and communicates the change the commit is introducing.

prompt: A ____ is the difference in changes between two commits, or saved changes. The ____ will visually describe what was added or removed from a file since its last commit.
explain: diff: A diff is the difference in changes between two commits, or saved changes. The diff will visually describe what was added or removed from a file since its last commit.
explainFull: diff: A diff is the difference in changes between two commits, or saved changes. The diff will visually describe what was added or removed from a file since its last commit.

prompt: ____ is an open source program for tracking changes in text files. It was written by the author of the Linux operating system, and is the core technology that GitHub, the social and user interface, is built on top of.
explain: Git: Git is an open source program for tracking changes in text files. It was written by the author of the Linux operating system, and is the core technology that GitHub, the social and user interface, is built on top of.
explainFull: Git: Git is an open source program for tracking changes in text files. It was written by the author of the Linux operating system, and is the core technology that GitHub, the social and user interface, is built on top of.

prompt: A text file containing information about the files in a repository that is typically the first file a visitor to your repository will see. A ____ file, along with a repository license, contribution guidelines, and a code of conduct, helps you share expectations and manage contributions to your project.
explain: README: A text file containing information about the files in a repository that is typically the first file a visitor to your repository will see. A README file, along with a repository license, contribution guidelines, and a code of conduct, helps you share expectations and manage contributions to your project.
explainFull: README: A text file containing information about the files in a repository that is typically the first file a visitor to your repository will see. A README file, along with a repository license, contribution guidelines, and a code of conduct, helps you share expectations and manage contributions to your project.

prompt: ____ are suggested improvements, tasks or questions related to the repository. ____ can be created by anyone (for public repositories), and are moderated by repository collaborators. Each ____ contains its own discussion thread. You can also categorize an ____ with labels and assign it to someone.
explain: issue: Issues are suggested improvements, tasks or questions related to the repository. Issues can be created by anyone (for public repositories), and are moderated by repository collaborators.
explainFull: issue: Issues are suggested improvements, tasks or questions related to the repository. Issues can be created by anyone (for public repositories), and are moderated by repository collaborators. Each issue contains its own discussion thread. You can also categorize an issue with labels and assign it to someone.

prompt: ____ allow others with access to your repository to comment on the changes proposed in pull requests, approve the changes, or request further changes before the pull request is merged.
explain: review: Reviews allow others with access to your repository to comment on the changes proposed in pull requests, approve the changes, or request further changes before the pull request is merged.
explainFull: review: Reviews allow others with access to your repository to comment on the changes proposed in pull requests, approve the changes, or request further changes before the pull request is merged.

prompt: Comments from collaborators on a pull request that approve the changes or request further changes before the pull request is merged.
explain: pull request review: Comments from collaborators on a pull request that approve the changes or request further changes before the pull request is merged.
explainFull: pull request review: Comments from collaborators on a pull request that approve the changes or request further changes before the pull request is merged.

prompt: The branch into which changes are combined when you merge a pull request. When you create a pull request, you can change the ____ from the repository's default branch to another branch if required.
explain: base branch: The branch into which changes are combined when you merge a pull request. When you create a pull request, you can change the base branch from the repository's default branch to another branch if required.
explainFull: base branch: The branch into which changes are combined when you merge a pull request. When you create a pull request, you can change the base branch from the repository's default branch to another branch if required.

prompt: The branch whose changes are combined into the base branch when you merge a pull request. Also known as the "compare branch."
explain: head branch: The branch whose changes are combined into the base branch when you merge a pull request. Also known as the "compare branch."
explainFull: head branch: The branch whose changes are combined into the base branch when you merge a pull request. Also known as the "compare branch."

prompt: The branch you use to create a pull request. This branch is compared to the base branch you choose for the pull request, and the changes are identified. When the pull request is merged, the base branch is updated with the changes from the ____. Also known as the "head branch" of the pull request.
explain: compare branch: The branch you use to create a pull request. This branch is compared to the base branch you choose for the pull request, and the changes are identified.
explainFull: compare branch: The branch you use to create a pull request. This branch is compared to the base branch you choose for the pull request, and the changes are identified. When the pull request is merged, the base branch is updated with the changes from the compare branch. Also known as the "head branch" of the pull request.

prompt: A branch used to experiment with a new feature or fix an issue that is not in production. Also called a topic branch.
explain: feature branch: A branch used to experiment with a new feature or fix an issue that is not in production. Also called a topic branch.
explainFull: feature branch: A branch used to experiment with a new feature or fix an issue that is not in production. Also called a topic branch.

prompt: A regular Git branch that is used by a developer to identify a conceptual line of development. Since branches are very easy and inexpensive, it is often desirable to have several small branches that each contain very well defined concepts or small incremental yet related changes. Can also be called a feature branch.
explain: topic branch: A regular Git branch that is used by a developer to identify a conceptual line of development. Since branches are very easy and inexpensive, it is often desirable to have several small branches that each contain very well defined concepts or small incremental yet related changes.
explainFull: topic branch: A regular Git branch that is used by a developer to identify a conceptual line of development. Since branches are very easy and inexpensive, it is often desirable to have several small branches that each contain very well defined concepts or small incremental yet related changes. Can also be called a feature branch.

prompt: You can use `git ____` on the command line to create a new branch, change your current working branch to a different branch, or even to switch to a different version of a file from a different branch with `git ____ [branchname] [path to file]`. The "____" action updates all or part of the working tree with a tree object or blob from the object database, and updates the index and HEAD if the whole working tree is pointing to a new branch.
explain: checkout: You can use `git checkout` on the command line to create a new branch, change your current working branch to a different branch, or even to switch to a different version of a file from a different branch with `git checkout [branchname] [path to file]`. The "checkout" action updates all or part of the working tree with a tree object or blob from the object database, and updates the index and HEAD if the whole working tree is pointing to a new branch.
explainFull: checkout: You can use `git checkout` on the command line to create a new branch, change your current working branch to a different branch, or even to switch to a different version of a file from a different branch with `git checkout [branchname] [path to file]`. The "checkout" action updates all or part of the working tree with a tree object or blob from the object database, and updates the index and HEAD if the whole working tree is pointing to a new branch.

prompt: A defined commit of a branch, usually the most recent commit at the tip of the branch.
explain: HEAD: A defined commit of a branch, usually the most recent commit at the tip of the branch.
explainFull: HEAD: A defined commit of a branch, usually the most recent commit at the tip of the branch.

prompt: Git will warn you if you're working on a ____, which means that Git is not pointing to a branch and that any commits you make will not appear in commit history. For example, when you check out an arbitrary commit that is not the latest commit of any particular branch, you're working on a "____."
explain: detached HEAD: Git will warn you if you're working on a detached HEAD, which means that Git is not pointing to a branch and that any commits you make will not appear in commit history. For example, when you check out an arbitrary commit that is not the latest commit of any particular branch, you're working on a "detached HEAD."
explainFull: detached HEAD: Git will warn you if you're working on a detached HEAD, which means that Git is not pointing to a branch and that any commits you make will not appear in commit history. For example, when you check out an arbitrary commit that is not the latest commit of any particular branch, you're working on a "detached HEAD."

prompt: When you ____ a pull request on GitHub, a new pull request is automatically opened, which has one commit that ____ the merge commit from the original merged pull request. In Git, you can ____ commits with `git ____`.
explain: revert: When you revert a pull request on GitHub, a new pull request is automatically opened, which has one commit that reverts the merge commit from the original merged pull request. In Git, you can revert commits with `git revert`.
explainFull: revert: When you revert a pull request on GitHub, a new pull request is automatically opened, which has one commit that reverts the merge commit from the original merged pull request. In Git, you can revert commits with `git revert`.

prompt: To reapply a series of changes from a branch to a different base, and reset the HEAD of that branch to the result.
explain: rebase: To reapply a series of changes from a branch to a different base, and reset the HEAD of that branch to the result.
explainFull: rebase: To reapply a series of changes from a branch to a different base, and reset the HEAD of that branch to the result.

prompt: To combine multiple commits into a single commit. Also a Git command.
explain: squash: To combine multiple commits into a single commit. Also a Git command.
explainFull: squash: To combine multiple commits into a single commit. Also a Git command.

prompt: To choose a subset of changes from a series of changes (typically commits) and record them as a new series of changes on top of a different codebase. In Git, this is performed by the `git cherry-pick` command to extract the change introduced by an existing commit on another branch and to record it based on the tip of the current branch as a new commit. For more information, see git-cherry-pick in the Git documentation.
explain: cherry-picking: To choose a subset of changes from a series of changes (typically commits) and record them as a new series of changes on top of a different codebase. In Git, this is performed by the `git cherry-pick` command to extract the change introduced by an existing commit on another branch and to record it based on the tip of the current branch as a new commit.
explainFull: cherry-picking: To choose a subset of changes from a series of changes (typically commits) and record them as a new series of changes on top of a different codebase. In Git, this is performed by the `git cherry-pick` command to extract the change introduced by an existing commit on another branch and to record it based on the tip of the current branch as a new commit. For more information, see git-cherry-pick in the Git documentation.

prompt: A ____ is a special type of merge where you have a revision and you are "merging" another branch's changes that happen to be a descendant of what you have. In such a case, you do not make a new merge commit but instead just update to this revision. This will happen frequently on a remote-tracking branch of a remote repository.
explain: fast-forward: A fast-forward is a special type of merge where you have a revision and you are "merging" another branch's changes that happen to be a descendant of what you have. In such a case, you do not make a new merge commit but instead just update to this revision.
explainFull: fast-forward: A fast-forward is a special type of merge where you have a revision and you are "merging" another branch's changes that happen to be a descendant of what you have. In such a case, you do not make a new merge commit but instead just update to this revision. This will happen frequently on a remote-tracking branch of a remote repository.

prompt: When your local copy of a repository is out-of-sync with the upstream repository and you need to fetch the upstream changes before you push your local changes.
explain: non-fast-forward: When your local copy of a repository is out-of-sync with the upstream repository and you need to fetch the upstream changes before you push your local changes.
explainFull: non-fast-forward: When your local copy of a repository is out-of-sync with the upstream repository and you need to fetch the upstream changes before you push your local changes.

prompt: A Git push that overwrites the remote repository with local changes without regard for conflicts.
explain: force push: A Git push that overwrites the remote repository with local changes without regard for conflicts.
explainFull: force push: A Git push that overwrites the remote repository with local changes without regard for conflicts.

prompt: When you successfully ____ to a remote repository, you update the remote branch with changes from your local branch. When you "____", Git will search for the branch's HEAD ref in the remote repository and verify that it is a direct ancestor to the branch's local HEAD ref. Once verified, Git pulls all objects (reachable from the local HEAD ref and missing from the remote repository) into the remote object database and then updates the remote HEAD ref. If the remote HEAD is not an ancestor to the local HEAD, the push fails.
explain: push a branch: When you successfully push a branch to a remote repository, you update the remote branch with changes from your local branch. When you "push a branch", Git will search for the branch's HEAD ref in the remote repository and verify that it is a direct ancestor to the branch's local HEAD ref.
explainFull: push a branch: When you successfully push a branch to a remote repository, you update the remote branch with changes from your local branch. When you "push a branch", Git will search for the branch's HEAD ref in the remote repository and verify that it is a direct ancestor to the branch's local HEAD ref. Once verified, Git pulls all objects (reachable from the local HEAD ref and missing from the remote repository) into the remote object database and then updates the remote HEAD ref. If the remote HEAD is not an ancestor to the local HEAD, the push fails.

prompt: When talking about a branch or a fork, the primary branch on the original repository is often referred to as the "____", since that is the main place that other changes will come in from. The branch/fork you are working on is then called the "downstream." Also called origin.
explain: upstream: When talking about a branch or a fork, the primary branch on the original repository is often referred to as the "upstream", since that is the main place that other changes will come in from. The branch/fork you are working on is then called the "downstream." Also called origin.
explainFull: upstream: When talking about a branch or a fork, the primary branch on the original repository is often referred to as the "upstream", since that is the main place that other changes will come in from. The branch/fork you are working on is then called the "downstream." Also called origin.

prompt: The default branch that is merged into the branch in question (or the branch in question is rebased onto). It is configured via `branch.<name>.remote` and `branch.<name>.merge`. If the ____ of A is origin/B sometimes we say "A is tracking origin/B."
explain: upstream branch: The default branch that is merged into the branch in question (or the branch in question is rebased onto). It is configured via `branch.<name>.remote` and `branch.<name>.merge`.
explainFull: upstream branch: The default branch that is merged into the branch in question (or the branch in question is rebased onto). It is configured via `branch.<name>.remote` and `branch.<name>.merge`. If the upstream branch of A is origin/B sometimes we say "A is tracking origin/B."

prompt: A ____ is a personal copy of another user's repository that lives on your account. ____ allow you to freely make changes to a project without affecting the original upstream repository. You can also open a pull request in the upstream repository and keep your ____ synced with the latest changes since both repositories are still connected.
explain: fork: A fork is a personal copy of another user's repository that lives on your account. Forks allow you to freely make changes to a project without affecting the original upstream repository.
explainFull: fork: A fork is a personal copy of another user's repository that lives on your account. Forks allow you to freely make changes to a project without affecting the original upstream repository. You can also open a pull request in the upstream repository and keep your fork synced with the latest changes since both repositories are still connected.

prompt: A repository that is used to track the same project but resides somewhere else.
explain: remote repository: A repository that is used to track the same project but resides somewhere else.
explainFull: remote repository: A repository that is used to track the same project but resides somewhere else.

prompt: The place where your code is stored: a repository on GitHub, another user's fork, or even a different server.
explain: remote URL: The place where your code is stored: a repository on GitHub, another user's fork, or even a different server.
explainFull: remote URL: The place where your code is stored: a repository on GitHub, another user's fork, or even a different server.

prompt: A working tree is ____ if it corresponds to the revision referenced by the current HEAD. Also see dirty.
explain: clean: A working tree is clean if it corresponds to the revision referenced by the current HEAD. Also see dirty.
explainFull: clean: A working tree is clean if it corresponds to the revision referenced by the current HEAD. Also see dirty.

prompt: A working tree is considered "____" if it contains modifications that have not been committed to the current branch.
explain: dirty: A working tree is considered "dirty" if it contains modifications that have not been committed to the current branch.
explainFull: dirty: A working tree is considered "dirty" if it contains modifications that have not been committed to the current branch.

prompt: Also known as SHA. A 40-character checksum hash that identifies the commit.
explain: commit ID: Also known as SHA. A 40-character checksum hash that identifies the commit.
explainFull: commit ID: Also known as SHA. A 40-character checksum hash that identifies the commit.

prompt: The user who makes the commit.
explain: commit author: The user who makes the commit.
explainFull: commit author: The user who makes the commit.

prompt: The "____" feature in Git describes the last modification to each line of a file, which generally displays the revision, author and time. This is helpful, for example, in tracking down when a feature was added, or which commit led to a particular bug.
explain: blame: The "blame" feature in Git describes the last modification to each line of a file, which generally displays the revision, author and time. This is helpful, for example, in tracking down when a feature was added, or which commit led to a particular bug.
explainFull: blame: The "blame" feature in Git describes the last modification to each line of a file, which generally displays the revision, author and time. This is helpful, for example, in tracking down when a feature was added, or which commit led to a particular bug.

prompt: The action of fixing up manually what a failed automatic merge left behind.
explain: resolve: The action of fixing up manually what a failed automatic merge left behind.
explainFull: resolve: The action of fixing up manually what a failed automatic merge left behind.

prompt: An invisible character or characters that symbolize the end of a line in a text file.
explain: line ending: An invisible character or characters that symbolize the end of a line in a text file.
explainFull: line ending: An invisible character or characters that symbolize the end of a line in a text file.

prompt: Git Large File Storage. An open source Git extension for versioning large files.
explain: LFS: Git Large File Storage. An open source Git extension for versioning large files.
explainFull: LFS: Git Large File Storage. An open source Git extension for versioning large files.

prompt: A ____ is a person with read and write access to a repository who has been invited to contribute by the repository owner.
explain: collaborator: A collaborator is a person with read and write access to a repository who has been invited to contribute by the repository owner.
explainFull: collaborator: A collaborator is a person with read and write access to a repository who has been invited to contribute by the repository owner.

prompt: A ____ is someone who does not have collaborator access to a repository but has contributed to a project and had a pull request they opened merged into the repository.
explain: contributor: A contributor is someone who does not have collaborator access to a repository but has contributed to a project and had a pull request they opened merged into the repository.
explainFull: contributor: A contributor is someone who does not have collaborator access to a repository but has contributed to a project and had a pull request they opened merged into the repository.

prompt: The user that is assigned to an issue.
explain: assignee: The user that is assigned to an issue.
explainFull: assignee: The user that is assigned to an issue.

prompt: A tag on an issue or pull request. Repositories come with a handful of default ____, but users can create custom ____.
explain: label: A tag on an issue or pull request. Repositories come with a handful of default labels, but users can create custom labels.
explainFull: label: A tag on an issue or pull request. Repositories come with a handful of default labels, but users can create custom labels.

prompt: A way to track the progress on groups of issues or pull requests in a repository.
explain: milestone: A way to track the progress on groups of issues or pull requests in a repository.
explainFull: milestone: A way to track the progress on groups of issues or pull requests in a repository.

prompt: GitHub's way of packaging and providing software to your users.
explain: release: GitHub's way of packaging and providing software to your users.
explainFull: release: GitHub's way of packaging and providing software to your users.

prompt: ____ block several features of Git on a branch that a repository administrator chooses to protect. They can't be force pushed, deleted, have changes merged without required checks passing or required reviews approved, or have files uploaded to it from the GitHub web interface. A ____ is usually the default branch.
explain: protected branch: Protected branches block several features of Git on a branch that a repository administrator chooses to protect. They can't be force pushed, deleted, have changes merged without required checks passing or required reviews approved, or have files uploaded to it from the GitHub web interface.
explainFull: protected branch: Protected branches block several features of Git on a branch that a repository administrator chooses to protect. They can't be force pushed, deleted, have changes merged without required checks passing or required reviews approved, or have files uploaded to it from the GitHub web interface. A protected branch is usually the default branch.

prompt: A restriction that repository admins can enable so that only certain users or teams can push or make certain changes to the branch.
explain: branch restriction: A restriction that repository admins can enable so that only certain users or teams can push or make certain changes to the branch.
